canonicalTopic: Its Not Ai and Its Not Superintelligence So What Is It

sourceSignals.query: Its Not Ai and Its Not Superintelligence So What Is It
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: When President Donald Trump addressed the United Nations in late September, he said the word “artificial” in "artificial intelligence" made the technology sound fake . Instead, he said, his government would start calling it “superintelligence,” or "SI." Not long after those remarks, the president made it official. He signed an executive order that instructed federal agencies to use his chosen phrase instead of AI in official communications. What Trump says goes: The Department of Justice has since told its staff to follow suit, and other government departments are likely to follow—not least because the president has now branded anyone calling it AI “THE ENEMY.” And it’s not just the government—the tech sector has responded to Trump’s pronouncement, too. Elon Musk said on October 4 that SpaceXAI would become SpaceXSI . The rebrand isn’t just Trump being Trump: AI’s capabilities have improved far beyond their previous limits since ChatGPT was first released in November 2022, and are reaching the point of superintelligence—a term that already means something in AI circles. (Superintelligence, in that telling, is the point at which AI systems can systematically outperform humans.) However, sticking the "superintelligence" label on a technology—when parts of it definitely don’t meet that standard yet—could make things worse by giving people a false sense of confidence and confusing them further. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he thought “superintelligence” was “a more accurate term” than the current branding of AI, though he doesn’t think people will find it “less scary.” An exclusive survey for Fast Company by market research firm Early Studies validates Altman’s perspective. A poll of approximately 1,000 people in the United States—which the firm says is a statistically representative sample of the population based on its methodology—found that only 1 in 9 people think the rebrand will have a positive effect on the U.S. Furthermore, 53% of Americans think people they know would not be comfortable calling the tech "superintelligence." Trump kinda has a point However, Trump’s unilateral action does raise a valid question about the term we currently use, and whether it’s suitable in the first place. AI has always been a bad way to describe a broad range of technologies. It dates back to a 1955 proposal by math professor John McCarthy and other academics for a Dartmouth College summer workshop held the following year. During the event, disparate researchers working to replicate the brain in silico (in or on a computer) agreed on "artificial intelligence" as a broad term to cover the full scope of their efforts. Seven decades later, it fits better than it did in the 1950s—but is still a highly disputed term. Tony Thorne, a lexicologist at King’s College London, says AI’s vagueness has helped the industry thrive—and the technology survive. “The term’s weaknesses—vague and imprecise, ambiguous since the first part looks negative and the second impressive or reassuring—are also its strengths,” he notes. The term’s use over the intervening decades has helped it stick in the minds of companies, governments, researchers, the media, and the public. A YouGov poll found 53% of Americans preferred "AI" as a way to describe the technology we’re currently using, compared with fewer than 10% who preferred Trump’s favored nomenclature. One reason might be who’s asking for the rebrand. Thorne thinks Trump’s alternative term is “boosterist” and “triumphalist”—two words that fit well with the entrepreneur-turned-politician but that but do nothing to tamp down strongly felt public anxiety about the technology. “Usage, not regulation, decides a word’s take-up and survival,” Thorne says. A technological misnomer  Still, some of those looking at the tech most closely think "AI" doesn’t work for the current technology, and arguably never did. Meredith Broussard, a professor at New York University’s Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute and author of Artificial Unintelligence: How Computers Misunderstand the World , objects to the second half of the phrase, not the first. “It’s extremely misleading to call it 'intelligence,’” she says. “It makes people think that there is a brain inside the machine, and there absolutely is not.” So a replacement term, Broussard reckons, ought to include the word “machine” and avoid “intelligence” entirely. Broussard also thinks technologists should stay out of the conversation. “People in tech are uniquely bad at choosing names,” Broussard points out. The proclivity to borrow names from science fiction or beloved popular culture is an obsession of tech bros, but it can also end up carrying over some of those associations onto the tech itself. Describing software as "intelligent" encourages people to attach human qualities to systems that don’t have them. Using words like “chat,” “bot,” and “agent” make complicated systems sound familiar, Thorne says. “Super” makes it sound like a superhero, adds Broussard—and that becomes worrying. As for alternative names, Broussard suggests “calculating machine” is accurate, even if tech PR teams might wince at the idea. Thorne would prefer something like “cognitive computing agent,” or "CCA," but is equally realistic about the prospects of it sticking. Whatever eventually replaces AI, if anything does, Broussard thinks it needs to avoid repeating the same mistake. “Any new name has to be firmly attached to reality.”

canonicalTopic: Googlebooks Mark the End of the Old Google

sourceSignals.query: Googlebooks Mark the End of the Old Google
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Does Google still believe in the open web? With the launch of its new Googlebooks, it doesn't feel that way. Googlebooks are Google's attempt to establish a new platform of Android-based laptops, with native Android app support and tight connectivity with Android phones. They're also an extension of Google's efforts to rebuild Android around AI , with Gemini features just a quick cursor gesture away. At the same time, Google plans to phase out ChromeOS, which it introduced in 2009 as a lightweight platform for the web. While Chromebooks remain popular in the education sector, Google says it will convert many existing models to Googlebooks, and it will end support for ChromeOS entirely by 2034. it's a sad end for what once represented Google at its most idealistic. Chromebooks weren't just a breakthrough in speed and simplicity for laptops, they were also a bold bet on the open web as the next great computing platform. As the web becomes more walled off, and Google pivots to a platform more directly under its control, that dream has finally run its course. How Chromebooks lost their way The original goal for Chrome OS was to strip away all the overhead of a traditional laptop to make computing faster and easier. Here's what Google wrote about the project in 2009 : "Speed, simplicity and security are the key aspects of Google Chrome OS. We're designing the OS to be fast and lightweight, to start up and get you onto the web in a few seconds. The user interface is minimal to stay out of your way, and most of the user experience takes place on the web. And as we did for the Google Chrome browser, we are going back to the basics and completely redesigning the underlying security architecture of the OS so that users don't have to deal with viruses, malware and security updates. It should just work." The first Chromebooks, which arrived in 2011, were basically just laptops that ran the Chrome browser, plus some extra window dressing. They had minimal internal storage and couldn't run regular desktop software, but this allowed them to stay nimble, with speedy boot times, frictionless software updates, and minimal risk of malware. If a user lost their Chromebook, they could simply set up a new one and pick up where they left off. In essence, Google was betting that nearly everything people did with their laptops would happen in a browser through sites like Gmail and Google Docs, so they could cut out all the other bloat to make those web apps shine. To that end, Google encouraged app makers to build for the open web, with applications that could run in any browser, Chromebooks included. Although Google maintained a "Chrome Web Store" for web apps and extensions, the platform was only limited by the web itself. Anything you could run in a browser, you could run on a Chromebook, and that benefitted Google because it meant more people were using its search engine to find things. "[A]ny time our users have a better computing experience [with Chrome OS], Google benefits as well by having happier users who are more likely to spend time on the Internet," the company wrote in its 2008 blog post. Over time, Google wavered on that original vision. It brought Android apps to Chrome OS in 2016, then added support for Linux apps in 2018. It even made a big foray into installable high-end gaming with Steam support . While these inclusions made Chromebooks more capable, they also added new layers of complexity and demanded laptops with more storage. Setting up a new Chromebook became more of an ordeal, and preserving security became a bigger challenge . In shifting away from laptops powered by the open web, Chrome OS became exactly the kind of heavyweight computing experience it was trying to replace. All this helped open the door for a new operating system built on Android instead. While Googlebooks will include a desktop-class version of Chrome, the emphasis now is on running Android apps and using AI. Meanwhile, the original tenets of ChromeOS have disappeared. Look through Google's announcement post for Googlebooks , and you will not find the words "speed," "simplicity," or "security" mentioned even once. Times have changed, and so has Google Google's pivot away from a web-based operating system shouldn't come as a major surprise. After all, Googlebooks are arriving at a time when the open web is destabilizing, in part because of Google itself. Along with other tech companies that are all-in on AI, Google is betting on a world where browsing the web is increasingly unnecessary . Instead of using Google Search as a gateway to other sites, Google intends to have AI generate whatever information you need. Instead of managing your own email inbox, chatbots like Gemini will manage it for you. Instead of visiting websites to shop or make restaurant reservations, AI companies want to deploy fleets of AI agents to navigate those sites on your behalf. As a result, using the web as a human is becoming more difficult. A growing number of websites are blocking themselves off from search engines and archival services in an attempt to keep AI crawlers out. Amazon has been limiting how many customer reviews some users can read because it thinks their behavior looks too robotic. Even just proving that you're not a bot requires increasingly complicated steps, as in Google's new ReCAPTCHA systems that demand phone-based verification or a recording of yourself performing hand gestures . It'd be wrong to say that Google's strategy with Chromebooks had anything to do with this. The company faltered on its original vision for a variety of other reasons, and the rise of AI would have been inevitable anyway. Still, the arrival of Googlebooks serves as one final reminder of what we've lost. There was a time when Google believed in the open web more than anything, and it was committed to a platform with no real boundaries. But that was back when getting folks to spend more time on the web was Google's ultimate goal. Googlebooks exist for a world in which Google is clawing back more of that time for itself.

There’s Markdown, an increasingly common way of formatting text using plain-text characters—Reddit and Discord both use this. And then there’s Slack, which for some reason uses its own formatting scheme entirely. The result? Copying and pasting text between apps often turns into a serious headache. There are detailed formatting guides for a variety of applications, meaning you can actually figure out how to format text properly in somewhere like Slack or WhatsApp. I admire any website that teaches its users to no longer need it, so I think this is a great addition. sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Unless you happen to live with a software engineer or avid gamer, you may not be aware of the current shortage in computer RAM —which your resident computer expert may be calling RAMageddon or the RAMpocalypse . The RAM shortage is a familiar story if you’ve ever dealt with capitalism. The demand for memory, specifically dynamic random access memory (DRAM), has increased dramatically because of the rise of AI data centers. AI companies have been buying up the global supply of these memory chips in anticipation of creating future networks. Unfortunately, the computer chip industry has not been able to scale up its supply, in part because of bottlenecks around certain specialized components that aren’t widely manufactured . The upshot is that computer memory chip prices have skyrocketed . Memory chips are now sold “ like lobsters in a restaurant ,” in that the prices are so volatile, they change from day to day. For most of us, this feels more like an academic concern than a problem that deserves to be called an apocalypse. Unless you are constructing your own personal computer or you’re a gamer who can no longer afford the latest gaming console , the high price of RAM seems pretty unrelated to your life. But when the cost of memory chips increases as much as fivefold in a short time, the downstream effects don’t remain localized to one industry. Here’s how surging RAM prices may affect your life. Memory, memory everywhere If this RAM shortage had occurred 30 years ago, the fallout would have almost exclusively affected personal computing and gaming. But the past three decades have seen the addition of computing power to everything from phones to stoves to tractors to litter boxes . And yes, each one of those “smart” devices needs RAM to work. The added cost of memory is already affecting the industries you might expect, starting with desktop PCs , laptops , and now phones . It’s now nearly impossible to find an affordable, entry-level version of these tech necessities. But that’s hardly the end of the price increase. Prices for tablets , smart devices , smart TVs , and even cars have all gone up recently because of the high cost of RAM. Industry experts anticipate similar price hikes for wearable devices and WiFi routers . To avoid price hikes, some companies have delayed the launch of highly-anticipated products. Most notably, Sony has delayed the PlayStation 6 to 2028 or later . With this long list of affected products, even the most tech-averse consumer will start to see the effects of the RAM shortage—possibly as early as this year’s holiday season, considering how commonly tech products appear on gift lists. The cybersecurity situation In addition to the economic fallout, the RAM shortage may also affect cybersecurity. According to an August report from J.P. Morgan Global Research , there are some critical vulnerabilities in the cybersecurity infrastructure that could be exacerbated by this memory shortage. Artificial intelligence data centers are consuming the majority of the available memory, which leaves the manufacturers of security hardware, firewalls, secure routers, and other cybersecurity needs with limited options and higher costs. That may lead to delayed upgrades and other important maintenance of cybersecurity infrastructure. As things stand, our national cybersecurity is not necessarily more vulnerable to attack than usual. But the J.P. Morgan report points out that a “nationwide cyberattack in the U.S. would unleash an estimated $145 billion in additional chip demand on a market already operating at full capacity.” Such a potential vulnerability should be enough to worry everyone, since it could theoretically increase prices for any sector that relies on cybersecurity—which is basically all of them . Surviving the RAMpocalypse Industry experts expect the RAM shortage to last for at least another two years —and possibly continue into 2030 . Since the average consumer can’t control global RAM production or AI data center memory usage, it may seem there’s little you can do about the shortage. But there are several strategies you may want to consider to protect yourself from RAMageddon, including: Reduce your RAM usage: Rather than upgrading your PC or laptop, try making the most of the RAM you already have. PCWorld recommends cutting down on background applications, which includes shutting down automated backup tools, chat apps, organizers, widgets, and the like. Plan your next tech purchase: Need to buy a laptop, graphics card, phone, or device? TechRadar suggests making your purchase sooner rather than later, since RAM prices are not projected to go down anytime soon. It may be worthwhile to wait for Black Friday sales, but if you need to replace or upgrade any tech, start making plans to purchase it soon. Reduce your AI usage: If consumers cut back on their AI usage, our collective action will push back on the current campaign to make this technology the center of our lives. Even if you already avoid AI wherever you can, here’s how to turn off the automatic AI in your search engines, internet browsers, and email accounts. Remember, this industry isn’t profitable yet , but it’s making other products much more expensive. Reducing your usage will help the AI industry set its expectations more reasonably—and maybe stop hogging all the memory. RAM, bam, thank you ma’am The cost of computer memory chips may seem much less urgent than the cost of fuel or food. But the global RAM shortage will have long-reaching implications in more industries than just computers and game consoles. Any kind of smart technology, from tablets to wearable devices to appliances, will likely see a price hike because of the high cost of RAM. This could affect the 2026 holiday shopping season, considering how common tech gifts have become. But there may be additional costs, considering the importance of RAM to our cybersecurity infrastructure. The continued high cost of memory could increase the vulnerabilities in cybersecurity since needed upgrades and other maintenance tasks may be delayed. The average consumer is not helpless in the face of this RAM shortage, however. Reducing your RAM usage to get more life out of your devices and planning your next tech purchase for the near future can help protect you from the financial fallout of the shortage, while cutting back on your AI usage may help the industry set more reasonable expectations.

canonicalTopic: Nobody Trusts Hr Its Up to Companies to Fix It

sourceSignals.query: Nobody Trusts Hr Its Up to Companies to Fix It
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Earlier this year, I wrote in Fast Company that 2026 could be the year companies finally begin taking employee well-being seriously. I also challenged HR leaders to seize the moment and help drive the requisite cultural change within their organizations. Many people subsequently reached out to me to argue that well-being cannot be just an HR initiative and that, to truly succeed, it requires the full buy-in and ownership of leaders at every level, including the C-suite. I found myself instantly agreeing with them. Back in January, my goal was to inspire HR leaders to make employee well-being a foundational value in their companies and to begin laying out how it could become institutionalized. But the more I thought about what that would require, the clearer it became that HR cannot embed well-being into how a company operates on its own. Responsibility must extend far beyond HR. The source of the problem For decades, companies have largely handed responsibility for the employee experience to Human Resources. It was HR that administered the engagement surveys, analyzed the results, and reported the findings. But the main drivers of employee engagement—workloads, caring and supportive leadership, flexibility, and job security—have always sat in the business itself, not HR. That's why engagement scores rarely moved. Leaders treated the data as HR's problem to fix, not their own. We're at risk of making the same mistake with well-being. Underneath that mismatch sits an untenable dual mandate: HR is expected to advocate for employees while simultaneously carrying out layoffs and job eliminations—decisions made by senior leadership, not HR. While the goal is for employees to trust HR to represent their interests, that trust erodes when those interests inevitably collide with business decisions. Data confirms the disconnect. Leapsome’s 2026 Workforce Trends Report found that 81% of HR leaders believe they successfully advocate for employees in business decisions, while only half (54%) of individual contributors fully trust HR to do so. Similarly, while 72% of HR leaders believe they can challenge top-down mandates, only 45% of individual contributors agree. Consequently, employee well-being needs to be managed the same way companies manage all other important business objectives. Someone at the top has to own it, managers must be accountable for it, employees need a continuous way to provide feedback—and there must be true consequences when line managers repeatedly fail to respond. Without those elements working together, well-being will remain something companies only talk about rather than something they systematically manage. Someone At The Top Has To Own It If we’ve learned anything from our decades of largely failed efforts to elevate employee engagement, it’s that the first step to making a serious and sustained commitment to employee well-being is putting someone at the top in charge. That person could be the Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO)—and in many companies, that may make the most sense. But if an organization creates a separate Chief Well-Being Officer, the position must be a genuine C-suite role with direct access to, and support from, the CEO and executive team. The title matters less than the authority behind it. If senior leaders don’t regard this person as a peer who can question decisions, escalate concerns, and influence what happens next, the position will have no teeth and zero impact. In 2022, Ernst & Young was one of the first companies to create the position of Chief Well-Being Officer. As a guest on my podcast recently, Frank Giampietro explained that in that position, his role is to systematically address the physical, emotional, financial, and social well-being of the firm's people—extending well beyond programs and resources to culture and the broader work environment. Not every organization needs another C-suite title, but every organization needs someone at the highest level who has both the responsibility and authority for employee well-being. Importantly, that leader must be involved before consequential decisions are made, not brought in afterward to explain them. Employees Need To Be Heard Continuously One of the great failures of employee engagement surveys has been that they were conducted only once or twice a year, and the data was often stale by the time it was digested and distributed to managers. Add in the fact that survey feedback was infrequently addressed, if ever, and workers naturally grew to distrust that their voices were ever being heard. In the future, companies should dispense with broad engagement surveys and replace them with shorter, more frequent pulse surveys that give leaders an immediate picture of how employees are experiencing work. Technology now makes it seamless to pose one or two focused questions and have responses almost instantly collated and summarized. A concise pulse survey tells a manager (and their manager) what is happening on their team right now—whether people feel valued, whether workday start and end boundaries are being honored, and whether employees feel personally supported. Asking targeted questions—such as whether people feel safe at work, whether they have autonomy and agency, if they trust the organization, or if they are hopeful about its future—gives leaders the immediate ability to see pain points before they metastasize. Listening like this, of course, can only be useful if the organization is prepared to respond; otherwise, the new survey becomes another useless and annoying ritual that asks employees for candor without giving them any reason to believe it will make a meaningful difference. Managers Have To Be Accountable For What They Hear Every manager should be expected to review feedback from their team, share what was learned, and discuss what can reasonably be changed. That must happen whether the feedback is positive or not, and when concerns cannot be addressed as employees would prefer. The manager’s boss—not HR—must make sure this happens. Making HR the police force would be a huge mistake as the person who supervises a manager is ultimately responsible for that manager's performance and leadership. As research shows, employee well-being is disproportionately influenced by workplace managers, and pulse surveys can identify those leaders whose teams repeatedly report they don’t feel valued, appreciated, trusted, or supported. In these cases, HR can help interpret the feedback and provide coaching, but the manager's own boss should be asking why the same concerns continue to surface. True to a company’s commitment to well-being, managers who show little willingness or ability to improve must ultimately be held accountable and weeded out. HR Should Own the System, Not the Outcome None of this makes HR less important. It is far more likely to make HR a more viable business partner because of its newly gained alignment with workplace managers. HR’s future role will be to implement and oversee the listening system, analyze patterns across teams, help managers interpret and respond to feedback, and identify problems individual managers cannot solve themselves. If numerous teams are reporting burnout, deteriorating relationships with managers, or distrust, HR can bring those trends into the executive conversation and ensure they are heard and acted upon, not overlooked. Ultimately, HR should own the system that allows the organization to understand employee well-being; leadership should own the outcome. Put Well-Being In The Room Before Decisions Are Made A critical pivot organizations now must make is to ensure that employee well-being is considered while major business decisions are being made—not after. When a company is contemplating layoffs, a major restructuring, a return-to-office mandate, or the deployment of AI that will fundamentally alter people's jobs, either the CHRO or Chief Well-Being Officer should be in the room asking what those decisions will mean for the people who have to live with them. That doesn’t mean well-being will always override financial or operational realities; businesses still must make difficult, painful decisions. But  how  those decisions are executed is a consideration routinely ignored today, as the drive for efficiency blinds leaders to both the short- and long-term implications of their choices. In recent years, research has consistently shown that caring for people and their well-being isn’t the drag on leadership performance we once imagined—it’s a major catalyst for it. So, when companies give C-suite authority to well-being, equip managers to listen continuously, and hold them accountable for the culture they create, HR can stop playing referee. Leadership starts in the heart, but it lives in how we manage human beings every single day. If we want employees to give us their best, we must fully commit to giving them ours.
